source.title: Graph Partitions: Recent Progresses and Some Open Problems

accepted.question_text: Let G be a triangle-free graph on n vertices. Can G always be made bipartite by deleting at most n^2/25 edges?

evidence.quote: Mentioning the bipartitions of triangle-free graphs, a long-standing conjecture of Erd˝os (see [10, p. 363] or [25]) is still open.

Conjecture 1.1 (Erd˝os’ Conjecture) Every triangle-free graph on n vertices can be made bipartite by removing at most n2
25 edges.

we usually call e(V1, V2, ··· , Vk) the size of the partition.

accepted.question_text: What is the computational complexity of the minimum bisection problem on weighted planar graphs, where a bisection is a bipartition whose two vertex classes have sizes as equal as possible?

evidence.quote: If ||Vi|−|Vj || ≤ 1 for any pair i, j ∈ {1, 2, ··· , k}, then we say that the partition is balanced. Balanced bipartition is usually referred to as bisection.

It is known that, on weighted planar graphs, the maximum bipartition problem is polynomial time solvable[31], but the maximum bisection problem is NP-hard, while the complexity of the minimum bisection problem remains unknown (see [37]).

accepted.question_text: Let G be a graph and M a maximum matching in G. A free neighbor of a vertex u not incident with M is a matched vertex x from an edge xy in M such that xu is an edge and yu is not an edge; two such unmatched vertices have different free-neighbor sets if these sets are unequal. Let r(M) be the maximum number of pairs of unmatched vertices such that each pair has different free-neighbor sets with respect to M, and let r(G) be the maximum r(M) over all maximum matchings M of G. Can r(G) be determined in polynomial time?

evidence.quote: Let M be a maximum matching of G. We use V (M) to denote the set of vertices incident with some edge of M. For xy ∈ M and u ̸∈ V (M), x is called a free neighbor of u if xu ∈ E(G) but yu ̸∈ E(G).

Let β(G) be the matching number (the size of a maximum matching) of G. For a maximum matching M, let r(M) be the maximum number of pairs of which each pair have different sets of free neighbors with respect to M, and let
r(G) = max{r(M); M runs over all maximum matchings of G}.

For any fixed M, r(M) can be determined polynomially. How about r(G)?
Problem 3.1 Can we determine r(G) polynomially?

accepted.question_text: For each integer k at least 1, what is the smallest constant c(k) such that every graph G with minimum degree delta(G) at least k has a bisection (S, T) for which both induced subgraphs G[S] and G[T] contain at most c(k)e(G) edges?

evidence.quote: Balanced bipartition is usually referred to as bisection.
Problem 3.2[13, Problem 7] What is the smallest constant c(k) such that every graph G with δ(G) ≥ k has a bisection of which each vertex class induces at most c(k)e(G) edges?

accepted.question_text: Does every graph G with m edges and minimum degree at least 2 admit a bisection (S, T) such that each of the two induced subgraphs G[S] and G[T] contains at most m/3 edges?

evidence.quote:
Conjecture 3.1[13, Conjecture 6] Every graph with m edges and minimum degree at least 2 admits a bisection of which each vertex class induces at most m
3 edges.
Employing also the idea of free neighbors from [40], Xu and Yu[71] confirmed Conjecture 3.1 and characterized the extremal graph.

Theorem 3.6[71] Every graph with m edges and minimum degree at least 2 admits a good bisection, i.e., a bisection (S, S¯) such that max{e(S), e(S¯)} ≤ m
3 . Moreover, the triangle K3 is the only extremal graph.

accepted.question_text: Let k be a positive integer. Can the o(m) term be removed from Lee et al.’s bisection theorem, so that every graph with m edges and minimum degree 2k or 2k + 1 has a bisection (S, T) satisfying max{e(S), e(T)} <= ((k + 1)/(2(2k + 1)))m?
accepted.context_brief: Removing o(m) from judicious bisection bound

evidence.quote:
Theorem 3.3[40] Every graph with m edges and minimum degree 2k or 2k + 1 admits a bisection (S, S) such that
max{e(S), e(S)} ≤ ( k + 1
2(2k + 1) + o(1) ) m.
Problem 3.3[40] Is it possible to remove the tail term o(m) in Theorem 3.3?

Following Theorem 3.4, one sees that if a graph G with m edges and minimum degree at least 2k or 2k + 1 does not admit bisection of which each class induces a subgraph with at most k+1
2(2k+1)m edges, then G is a sparse graph.

accepted.question_text: Does every planar graph with n vertices admit a bisection (S, T) whose cut size e(S, T), the number of edges with one endpoint in each part, is at most n?

evidence.quote: There are still some interesting minimum bisection problems particularly on special families of graphs. Here below is a still open folklore conjecture on the minimum bisection of planar graphs.

Conjecture 3.2[28] Every planar graph of order n has a bisection (S, S¯) such that e(S, S¯) ≤
n.

accepted.question_text: Does every graph G admit a bisection (S, T) such that for every vertex u in S, the number of neighbors of u in T is at least d_S(u) - 1, and for every vertex v in T, the number of neighbors of v in S is at least d_T(v) - 1?

evidence.quote: We complete this section with a wildly open conjecture of Bollob´as and Scott [13].

Conjecture 3.3[13, Conjecture 8] Every graph G admits a bisection (S, S¯) with
|NS¯(u)| ≥ dS(u) − 1 for each u ∈ S,
and
|NS(v)| ≥ dS¯(v) − 1 for each v ∈ S. ¯

accepted.question_text: Does there exist an absolute constant c such that every graph G admits a bisection (S, T) with |N_T(u)| >= d_S(u) - c for every u in S and |N_S(v)| >= d_T(v) - c for every v in T?

evidence.quote:
There is almost no progress on this conjecture as I know. Even a constant c is not known such that every graph G has a bisection S, S¯ with
|NS¯(u)| ≥ dS(u) − c for each u ∈ S,
and
|NS(v)| ≥ dS¯(v) − c for each v ∈ S. ¯

accepted.question_text: For positive integers s and t, let f(s,t) be the least connectivity threshold such that every f(s,t)-connected graph can be partitioned into two sets S and T for which the induced subgraphs G[S] and G[T] have connectivity at least s and t, respectively. Is f(s,t) always equal to s + t + 1?

evidence.quote: In 1982, Gy˝ori[32, 63] proposed a problem as follows: for given positive integers s and t, is there an integer f(s, t) such that the vertex set of every f(s, t)-connected graph can be partitioned into two sets S and T which induce subgraphs of connectivity at least s and t respectively?

Then Thomassen made the following
Conjecture 4.1[63] g(s, t) = s + t + 1, and f(s, t) = s + t + 1.
The latter part of Conjecture 4.1 is still open. The best bound f(s, t) ≤ 4s + 4t − 13 is due to Hajnal [32].

accepted.question_text: For positive integers s and t, let g(s,t) be the least minimum-degree threshold such that every graph with minimum degree at least g(s,t) can be partitioned into S and T with delta(G[S]) at least s and delta(G[T]) at least t. On triangle-free graphs, is the sharp threshold g(s,t) equal to s + t?

evidence.quote: He showed essentially that for positive integers s and t, there is an integer g(s, t) such that the vertex set of every graph G with minimum degree at least g(s, t) can be partitioned into S and T which induce subgraphs of minimum degree at least s and t, respectively
Then Stiebitz asked a question: is it true that, for any positive integers s and t, g(s, t) = s + t on triangle-free graphs?
With the same technique of Stiebitz, Kaneko[35] answered the question affirmatively and proved that if s ≥ 1 and t ≥ 1, then g(s, t) ≤ s + t on triangle-free graphs.

accepted.question_text: Let G be a triangle-free graph with no K_{2,3} subgraph, and let a and b be integer-valued functions on V(G) such that a(x) >= 2, b(x) >= 2, and d(x) >= a(x) + b(x) - 1 for every vertex x. Must V(G) have a partition (A, B) such that every x in A has at least a(x) neighbors inside A and every y in B has at least b(y) neighbors inside B?
accepted.context_brief: Degree partition for triangle-free K2,3-free graphs

evidence.quote: Theorem 4.3[47] Let G be a triangle-free graph in which no two quadrilaterals share edges, and a, b two integral functions on V (G) such that a(x) ≥ 2 and b(x) ≥ 2 for each vertex x of G. If d(x) ≥ a(x) + b(x) − 1 for each vertex x of G, then G admits a partition (A, B) such that dA(x) ≥ a(x) for each x ∈ A, and dB(y) ≥ b(y) for each y ∈ B.
It would be nice if someone can strengthen Theorem 4.3 to triangle-free and K2,3-free graphs.

accepted.question_text: For every positive integer l, does there exist an integer k(l) such that whenever G is a k(l)-connected graph and X is a subset of V(G) with |X| <= l, the graph G has a partition (S, T) with X contained in S, every vertex of S having at least l neighbors in T, and both induced subgraphs G[S] and G[T] l-connected?
accepted.context_brief: Thomassen partition with prescribed small set

evidence.quote: K¨uhn and Osthus’ theorem is a step toward to a very hard conjecture of Thomassen [63].

Conjecture 4.2[63] For every integer l, there is an integer k = k(l) such that if G is a k-connected graph and X ⊆ V (G) with |X| ≤ l, then G admits a partition (S, T ) such that X ⊆ S, each vertex in S has at least l neighbors in T and both G[S] and G[T ] are l-connected.
Little is known about this conjecture.

accepted.question_text: For every natural number l at least 3, does there exist an integer f(l) such that for any two vertices x and y in any f(l)-connected graph G, there is an induced path P from x to y for which the vertex-deleted graph G - V(P) is l-connected?
accepted.context_brief: Lovasz induced path with connected complement

evidence.quote: Conjecture 4.3[63] For each natural number l, there exists an integer f(l) such that, for any two vertices x and y in an f(l)-connected graph G, there exists an induced xy-path P such that G − V (P) is l-connected.
It is easy to verify that f(1) = 3 by Tutte’s wheel theorem. Kriesell[38] and Chen et al.[19] independently proved that f(2) = 5. For k ≥ 3, f(k) is not known.

accepted.question_text: For given integers s and t, does there exist an integer l such that every graph with minimum degree at least l has a bisection (S, T) satisfying delta(G[S]) >= s and delta(G[T]) >= t? If such l exists, what is the smallest such threshold gb(s,t)?
accepted.context_brief: Existence of bisection degree threshold gb(s,t)

evidence.quote: Recall that a bisection is a bipartition of which the two subsets have size as equal as possible.

Can we have an analogue of Stiebitz’s theorem in bisections? In other words, for given integers s and t, is there an integer l such that every graph with minimum degree at least l has a bisection (S, T ) with δ(G[S]) ≥ s and δ(G[T ]) ≥ t? If such a constant does exist, we use gb(s, t) to denote the smallest one[45].

accepted.question_text: Let s be a positive integer. Does every graph with minimum degree at least 2s + 1 admit a bisection (S, T) such that both induced subgraphs G[S] and G[T] have minimum degree at least s?

evidence.quote: In the light of the connection to Conjecture 3.3, we propose the following, perhaps easier, question on gb(s, s).
Problem 4.1[45] Let s be a positive integer. Is it true that every graph with minimum degree at least 2s + 1 admits a bisection (S, T ) such that min{δ(G[S]), δ(G[T ])} ≥ s?
If the answer is YES, then the bound is best possible as evidenced by the complete graph K2s+1.

accepted.question_text: Does every graph G with minimum degree at least 4 admit a 2-good partition (S, T), meaning min{delta(G[S]), delta(G[T])} >= 2, whose two class sizes are nearly balanced in the sense that floor(|V(G)|/2) - 2 <= |S| <= |T| <= ceil(|V(G)|/2) + 2?

evidence.quote: Arkin and Hassin[4] also proposed a conjecture.

Conjecture 4.4[4, Conjecture 7] Each graph G with δ(G) ≥ 4 admits a 2-good partition (S, T ) such that floor( 1
2 |V (G)|) − 2 ≤ |X|≤|Y |≤ceil( 12 |V (G)|) + 2.
It should be mentioned that the conjecture is not always true since in any partition (S, T ) of K5, min{δ(G[S]), δ(G[T ])} ≤ 1.

needs_review.question_text_raw: Therefore, the problem of finding Edwards’ type bound on maximum/minimum bisections remains open.

evidence.quote: Both of the two bounds are not Edwards’ types, because no function on m and n can bound β(G) (although β(G) is polynomial time computable), and the computation of r(G) is still open. Therefore, the problem of finding Edwards’ type bound on maximum/minimum bisections remains open.

needs_review.question_text_raw: After Stiebitz’s theorem, it is natural to ask for similar conditions guaranteeing the existence of a bipartition (S, T) such that G[S], G[T] and (S, T)G have large minimum degree simultaneously.

evidence.quote: After Stiebitz’s theorem, it is natural to ask for similar conditions guaranteeing the existence of a bipartition (S, T ) such that G[S], G[T ] and (S, T )G ((S, T )G denotes the bipartite subgraph obtained from G by removing all edges in G[S] and G[T ]) have large minimum degree simultaneously. K¨uhn and Osthus[39] answered this question negatively.

trace.notes: Normalized the single input as a zbMATH resolver URL for document id 6634250. The zbMATH API identified the exact work as Baogang Xu, "Graph partitions: recent progresses and some open problems," Adv. Math. (Beijing) 45(1), 1-20 (2016), with DOI 10.11845/sxjz.2015001a. Exact-title recovery found the CCJ/Peking University PDF with matching title, author, journal, issue, year, and DOI. A direct shell download attempt of the CCJ PDF failed with DNS resolution for ccj.pku.edu.cn, so extraction used the readable PDF text from the resolved CCJ URL rather than metadata or snippets.

Mapped a 20-page PDF. Page 1 gives title, author, abstract, graph notation, and degree notation. Page 2 defines k-partitions, edge counts e(V_i), e(V_i,V_j), and partition size. Section 1 covers maximum partitions and contains open conjectures on triangle-free graphs, high-girth examples, and connected k-partitions. Section 2 covers judicious partitions, anti-Cheeger constants, Problem 2.1, and Conjecture 2.1. Section 3 covers bisections and contains computational, extremal, and local bisection problems. Section 4 covers partitions with degree constraints and contains Gyori-Thomassen, Stiebitz/Kaneko, Kuhn-Osthus, Thomassen, Lovasz, and bisection-with-degree-constraints questions.

Extracted explicit and implicit open questions from Section 1: the Erdos triangle-free deletion bound, its asymptotic ratio form, Alon et al.’s high-girth extremal construction conjecture, and Bollobas-Scott’s connected k-partition lower-bound conjecture.
Extracted the anti-Cheeger multi-way inequality question, Problem 2.1 on simultaneous k-partition bounds, and Conjecture 2.1 on pair-union edge counts in k-partitions.

Extracted bisection questions on weighted planar minimum bisection complexity, computing r(G), judicious bisection constants c(k), the solved minimum-degree-2 judicious bisection conjecture, removal of o(m) in Lee et al.’s theorem, planar minimum bisections, and Bollobas-Scott local bisection inequalities.

Extracted degree-constraint partition questions: the open connectivity threshold f(s,t), the solved triangle-free degree threshold g(s,t), the proposed strengthening to triangle-free K_{2,3}-free graphs, Thomassen’s and Lovasz’s connectivity conjectures, the existence of bisection thresholds gb(s,t), Problem 4.1, and the Arkin-Hassin 2-good partition conjecture resolved negatively by K5.
Rewrote Erdos’ triangle-free conjecture as a standalone edge-deletion-to-bipartite question.
Expanded the source’s ratio language into the asymptotic deletion statement for every epsilon and all sufficiently large n.
Restricted the high-girth extremal construction question to r at least 6 because the source states r=4 and r=5 are already known.
Expanded k-partition size using the source definitions of partition size and edge counts.
Inlined h(m), the cross-edge lower bound, and the maximum induced-part upper bound from equations (1.2) and (2.1).
Expanded the pair-union edge-count conjecture and preserved the high-minimum-degree clause about removing O(n).
Recast the source’s unknown-complexity sentence as a computational complexity question and included the bisection definition.
Expanded free neighbor, r(M), and r(G) definitions before posing the polynomial-time computability question.
Expanded Problem 3.2 into the smallest-constant c(k) formulation with induced-edge bounds on both sides of a bisection.
Preserved Conjecture 3.1 and marked it solved because the source explicitly says Xu and Yu confirmed it in Theorem 3.6.
Resolved the reference to Theorem 3.3 by stating the min-degree hypothesis and the target bound without the o(m) term.
Expanded the planar minimum-bisection folklore conjecture with the cut-size notation.
Rewrote Bollobas-Scott’s local bisection inequalities using S,T notation and explicit neighbor-count meanings.
Separated the weaker absolute-constant version from the c=1 conjecture because it asks for any universal error constant.
Focused Conjecture 4.1 on the unresolved connectivity threshold f(s,t), since the source says the degree threshold part is confirmed.
Kept Stiebitz’s triangle-free threshold question as a solved historical item because the source explicitly says Kaneko answered it affirmatively.
Expanded the proposed strengthening of Theorem 4.3 by restating the graph restrictions, function hypotheses, and desired partition.
Rewrote Thomassen’s Conjecture 4.2 with the prescribed set X and l-connectivity requirements inline.
Restricted Lovasz’s conjecture to l at least 3 because the source states f(1) and f(2) are known.
Expanded the bisection analogue of Stiebitz’s theorem and the definition of gb(s,t).
Rewrote Problem 4.1 as the s-good bisection threshold question at minimum degree 2s+1.
Rewrote Arkin-Hassin’s conjecture with the 2-good condition and balance window; marked solved because the source gives K5 as a counterexample.
